confidence_why: Chao 1947 states outright that stress never affects the identity of a Cantonese word, Lee 1993 and Wong, Chan and Beckman 2005 independently deny any contrast between stressed and unstressed syllables, and the only hint of word stress, an iambic pattern Bauer, Cheung, Cheung and Ng 2004 suspected from the duration of two personal names, is one they say they did not investigate.

catalog_quote: 13. Stress. — Stress is not a constituting element of words in Cantonese as it is in Mandarin or English. Of course all syllables in Cantonese are not pronounced with the same degree of force or heard with the same degree of loudness. But the variation depends upon the sounds concerned and upon the relative prominence of words in the sentence determined by stylistic factors. The identity of words in Cantonese is never affected by stress.

sweep_summary: Yue Chinese/Cantonese is not in the catalog. Of the five stress-title items, none is a first-hand word-stress description: Williams 1856 'Tonic Dictionary' (downloaded from archive.org) is about tones and only separates tone from 'accent'; Lee et al. 2024 (abstract, paywalled) is child bilingual intonation; Bauer, Cheung, Cheung & Ng 2004 (downloaded from the SEALang SALA archive and scanned, 21 pp.) is about sentence-level focus-stress (duration is the main cue) with a tentative side remark that bisyllabic words 'may carry inherent word-stress on the second syllable' (pp. 35-36, 39); Wong, Chan & Beckman 2005 (paywalled OUP; abstract via Crossref) states the 'absence of contrast between stressed and reduced (neutral tone) syllables' and is the one item worth acquiring in full (priority high); the Glottolog 'Jun 2005' entry is a duplicate of that chapter credited to the compilers. The best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title remains Chao 1947 Cantonese Primer p. 36 (already held by the project): 'Stress is not a constituting element of words in Cantonese.. The identity of words in Cantonese is never affected by stress' -> no-word-stress.org, Crossref, Unpaywall and the SALA archive index.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Cantonese is a tone language (six to nine tones plus the derived 'changed tone' pinn'iam) in which stress plays no role at the word level: there is no lexically or positionally fixed word stress, and no word is distinguished by stress. Perceived loudness differences between syllables follow from the segments themselves and from sentence-level prominence set by stylistic (focus/emphasis) factors.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Chao contrasts Cantonese explicitly with Mandarin (where neutral tone / stress is word-constituting) and English.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level explicitly denied; prominence is sentence-level and stylistic. Later instrumental work (Lee et al. 2002, saved) finds word-final rime lengthening with slightly higher F0/intensity on non-final syllables but does not call this stress; FSI 1970 speaks only of sentence stress. Chao describes the Canton (Guangzhou) standard as taught at Harvard in 1942-47.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Chao 1947 describes standard Cantonese of Canton (Guangzhou) as taught at Harvard 1942-47; Zee 1991, Lee et al. 2002, Wong 2004 and Man 2002 describe Hong Kong Cantonese. Both are the Guangzhou-Hong Kong standard variety of Yue (yuec1235 is the language-level code; Glottolog has no separate accepted glottocode for standard Cantonese distinct from Yue). The statement does not cover other Yue lects (Taishan/Siyi, Nanning Baihua, Tengxian) listed in Glottolog's yuec1235 bibliography.

She adds (citing Hashimoto 1972 and Kiu 1977) that the perceived prominence is a function of tone, not of position, and that Cantonese loanword phonology maps English stress onto the high tone. new_statements.rule_in_words: Cantonese is a tone language with a phonetic stress difference that is never lexically contrastive; following Hashimoto 1972, syllables carrying the high tones (35, 53/55, high entering 5) are perceived as more heavily stressed than syllables with other tones, and in English loanwords the English stressed syllable is rendered with the high level tone (55/53), an unstressed word-final syllable with the changed tone 35, other unstressed syllables with 33. No positional word-stress rule is given.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Hong Kong Cantonese is treated as a tone language without a word-stress system: it has no neutral-tone (reduced) syllables, the author finds no reliable phonological markers comparable to Mandarin 'stress' or to a dominant sandhi syllable, and she argues that syllable-fusion facts do not warrant positing an underlying trochaic (Chan 1985) or iambic (Lee 2003) word-stress pattern; the bisyllabic 'foot' she invokes is a pure grouping unit (C_ToBI), not a prominence unit, and in fusion neither syllable is 'dominant' (tone is the last thing to go).

tone_statements.quote: Cantonese is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken in Hong Kong, Macau, and Guangzhou (Eberhard et al., 2020). It has six lexical tones that occur on open syllables with optional nasal codas (Bauer & Benedict, 1997; Matthews & Yip, 2013). [...] These lexical tones are distinguished by pitch height, contour, and magnitude of change (Fok, 1974; Gandour, 1981; Khouw & Ciocca, 2007). Among these six tones, there are three level tones (T1, T3, T6), two rising tones (T2, T5), and one falling tone (T4). The level tones mainly differ in pitch height: T1 has the highest pitch, followed by T3, followed by T6, which has the lowest pitch. The rising tones are characterized by a rising contour, with T2 ending at a higher pitch than T5. Finally, the falling tone, T4, is produced with a falling contour and typically contains considerable glottalization (Yu & Lam, 2014).

readall_conflicts: No contradiction. The catalog's statement of record (Chao 1947: stress is not a constituting element of words; 41-42: Cantonese 'has stress, but does not use it contrastively'; heavier stress is perceived on high-tone syllables, after Hashimoto 1972) both deny lexically contrastive word stress in a tone language. The only difference is terminological: Chao frames the non-contrastive force differences as segment- and sentence-dependent, Lee/Hashimoto tie them to tone height. Neither gives a positional rule, so the tentative iambic word-stress remark from Bauer et al. 2004 (earlier reading, two test words, 'not investigated') remains unsupported by any of the six works here. Four of the six works could not be opened (Wong 2006, Kwan 2005, Wong S.Y. 2005, Lam 2004); Wong 2002 was opened and is silent.

sources.quote: Cantonese is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken in Hong Kong, Macau, and Guangzhou (Eberhard et al., 2020). It has six lexical tones that occur on open syllables with optional nasal codas (Bauer & Benedict, 1997; Matthews & Yip, 2013). [...] These lexical tones are distinguished by pitch height, contour, and magnitude of change (Fok, 1974; Gandour, 1981; Khouw & Ciocca, 2007). Among these six tones, there are three level tones (T1, T3, T6), two rising tones (T2, T5), and one falling tone (T4). The level tones mainly differ in pitch height: T1 has the highest pitch, followed by T3, followed by T6, which has the lowest pitch. The rising tones are characterized by a rising contour, with T2 ending at a higher pitch than T5. Finally, the falling tone, T4, is produced with a falling contour and typically contains considerable glottalization (Yu & Lam, 2014).
